newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Credit Lyonnais seeks new bailout.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Credit Lyonnais seeks new bailout.

text.p: State-owned Credit Lyonnais, which once set out to fulfil a government dream of putting French banking on the world map, was poised on Friday for another huge bailout aimed at finally rescuing it from an ill-fated investment binge.

The government, about to seek European Commission approval for its third rescue attempt in four years, has refused to put a price tag on the package that should ready Credit Lyonnais for privatisation.

But the Commission, which only two years ago approved 45 billion francs ($7.9 billion) in aid for the bank, has said it may need up to 30 billion francs more to put the once "grand old lady" of French banking back on an even keel.
The fresh call on the state purse by Credit Lyonnais, which briefly became the biggest bank outside Japan during the 1980s, comes amid reports it is headed for a spectacular profit rebound this year.
This has provoked fury from rival Societe Generale which has called for a "controlled liquidation" of the bank, saying the taxpayer should not pick up the tab for its losses.
The profits recovery is also expected to provoke tough questions from the EU, which has already said it is alarmed by the vast amounts of public money poured into the bank.
The crisis has forced the government, struggling to ready France for monetary union, to confront Paris's traditional way of doing business in which the state has played a dominant role.
"I hope this revolting experience will pass the message to the nation that the state...should not be a shareholder (in companies)," Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said this week.
Credit Lyonnais launched its ill-fated expansion drive under the previous Socialist administration, which was keen to ensure French banks could compete against their international rivals.
"The French banking system is a non-profit making system ...a very old culture of doing banking like an administration," Jean-Baptiste Bellon, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said.

Now, the centre-right government is determined to end the drain on public funds through a big programme of privatisation. It has pledged to privatise the bank as soon as possible but needs to put fresh money into it first to make it saleable.

The Commission, expected to get its first look at the French plan next week, has said 30 billion francs will be needed. That would cover losses on sales of assets bought at the market's peak and soften the terms of a loan the bank made under a 1995 state bailout to finance the spinoff of dud assets from its balance sheet.
But people close to the affair say that does not include the cost of boosting the bank's solvency ratios to international standards. This could push the amount even higher.
And still, no one knows the ultimate cost of the rescue of the bank, known as "Crazy Lyonnais" in its lending heyday.
"We will not know this for many years," Arthuis said. Some officials say the total bill could top 100 billion francs.

In funding the bank -- the worst of a series of state firms needing state cash -- the government must avoid increasing its budget deficit, which it must cut to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year to qualify for European monetary union.
In theory, all such funding must come from the government's privatisation revenues of which the biggest this year will be the partial sale of France Telecom for at least 25 billion francs.
The latest rescue talks have been conducted amid bitterness on all sides with the government blaming its predecessors for the bank's troubles.
The Commission once accused the bank of engaging in a "bulimia of investments and acquisitions," bent on becoming the French equivalent of Germany's mighty Deutsche Bank.
Under its former chairman, Jean-Yves Haberer, the bank built up a vast array of real estate loans just before the bottom fell out of the French property market in mid-1990.
It lent heavily to businesses which got hammered by the recession, and lent generously abroad, getting burned by, among others, disgraced British newspaper tycoon Robert Maxwell.
It also, via an ill-fated loan to Italian businessman Giancarlo Paretti, became the reluctant owner of Hollywood film studio Metro-Goldwyn Mayer, which it finally sold last year.
Haberer, fired in 1993, alleged some of the most disastrous loans were at the behest of the Socialists which wanted to help friends such as Maxwell and Parretti.
When the economy slid into recession, politicians urged the bank to keep lending to protect jobs, worsening its problems.

Haberer's replacement, Jean Peyrelevade, has pledged the bank to turn the bank into a medium-sized institution confined to retail and investment operations in France and merchant banking and capital market activities internationally.
Ironically, some of his restructuring is bearing fruit. One newspaper said on Thursday the bank, which lost 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994, would earn 3.4 to 3.7 billion francs this year.
The Commission has said it will take three to four months to decide on the latest bailout. ($ = 5.691 French Francs)
